articles.title: Val Kilmer turned a 5,328-acre New Mexico ranch into a retreat with rental cabins and a B&B; he asked $33 million in 2009, then sold most of the property two years later when the asking price fell to $18.5 million
articles.summary: Val Kilmer’s sprawling Pecos River ranch in New Mexico went from a private Hollywood escape to a high-end hospitality retreat before eventually changing
articles.body: Val Kilmer’s sprawling Pecos River ranch in New Mexico went from a private Hollywood escape to a high-end hospitality retreat before eventually changing hands in 2011. Contemporary reports from CBS News and the Associated Press, along with real-estate publications including The Land Report, documented the property’s years-long journey from a $33 million listing to its eventual sale after a steep reduction in the asking price.Located about 22 miles northeast of Santa Fe in San Miguel County, the ranch stretched across 5,328 acres and followed a particularly scenic section of the Pecos River. The property was known for its river frontage, natural springs, wildlife and extensive trails through New Mexico’s high-desert landscape. A later account from Realtor.com described the ranch as largely wild, with canyons and pine forests surrounding its residential buildings.Kilmer had acquired the land in the 1990s and spent years developing it into a secluded base away from Hollywood. Earlier coverage by the Los Angeles Times described the ranch as containing guest cottages, staff quarters, stables, barns and corrals, while Kilmer kept horses and other animals on the property. He had also previously attempted to sell portions of the ranch, including an approximately 1,800-acre section listed for $18 million in 2006.By 2009, Kilmer had changed strategy and put the entire ranch on the market. The Land Report reported an asking price of $33 million, with the property offering several homes and outbuildings as well as more than five miles of Pecos River frontage. The listing represented a significant escalation from his earlier attempts to sell smaller portions of the ranch.The property’s price subsequently dropped sharply. By late 2010, reports said the ranch had been reduced to $18.5 million, down from $23 million earlier that year. The AP also reported that the ranch included more than 10 natural springs, hiking and riding trails, guest quarters and a large main residence.The ranch was not simply a private residence. Kilmer had sought permission to operate guesthouses as overnight accommodations, eventually receiving approval from San Miguel County after controversy surrounding remarks he had previously made about the region. The Los Angeles Times reported that the proposed lodging involved three guesthouses, while contemporary coverage described the property as operating as a bed-and-breakfast with rental cabins.Its history also extended well beyond Kilmer. The land formed part of the larger Forked Lightning Ranch associated with oilman Buddy Fogelson and actress Greer Garson. According to the National Park Service, Fogelson purchased the original 5,500-acre ranch in 1941, and he and Garson later used it as a residence and gathering place for prominent figures from Hollywood and beyond. After Fogelson’s death, the property was divided among his heirs, with portions eventually passing to Kilmer and actress Jane Fonda.After several years on the market, most of Kilmer’s Pecos River property was finally sold in 2011. CBS News reported that the buyer was Texas oil and gas executive Benjamin A. Strickling III and his wife, Roxann. The deed transfer was recorded on September 30, 2011, according to contemporary property reports. The $18.5 million figure represented a dramatic reduction from Kilmer’s original $33 million asking price, amounting to roughly 44% below the initial listing.The sale marked the end of Kilmer’s long chapter on the Pecos River, where he had built not just a home but a sprawling private retreat around the landscape. The property later remained associated with conservation and outdoor recreation, while the larger historic Forked Lightning Ranch continues to be preserved in part through Pecos National Historical Park.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2012, Markiplier raised $1,000 in a 24-hour charity stream; six years later, one unusual calendar project alone generated $500,000 for cancer research
articles.summary: Mark Fischbach, better known online as Markiplier, was still building his YouTube audience when he first discovered how much his platform could do for
articles.body: Mark Fischbach, better known online as Markiplier, was still building his YouTube audience when he first discovered how much his platform could do for charity. In July 2012, he had around 2,000 subscribers when he decided to game for 24 hours and raise $1,000 for Child’s Play. He reached the target and saw how his small but growing community could come together for a cause. Six years later, a much larger audience would help him raise an extraordinary amount for cancer research.In Feb. 2013, Markiplier raised $8,047 for the Cancer Research Institute through a gaming livestream. His connection to the cause was also personal. His father had been diagnosed with lung cancer during Mark’s senior year of high school and died shortly afterward. By March 2018, Markiplier had reached a new milestone with more than 20 million subscribers. To celebrate, he followed through on a promise and created an unusual calendar that raised $500,000 for CRI in just two days.Markiplier started with a $1,000 charity goal when he had around 2,000 subscribersMarkiplier's first major charity stream came when his YouTube career was still in its early stages. In July 2012, he had around 2,000 subscribers. He decided to play games for 24 hours and set a $1,000 fundraising goal for Child’s Play.The challenge gave Mark an early look at what his audience could accomplish when it came together for a charitable cause. He reached the $1,000 target and continued to build his channel after the fundraiser.His charity work soon became bigger. In February 2013, Markiplier held another gaming livestream and raised $8,047 for the Cancer Research Institute. The fundraiser took less than nine hours.Cancer research had a personal connection for Mark. His father had been diagnosed with lung cancer while Mark was in his senior year of high school. He died shortly afterward.“It’s one of the hardest things anyone can go through,” Mark later told CRI.That experience stayed with him as his online audience grew. Mark also wanted his charity work to encourage other people to support causes they cared about. In his interview with CRI, he said, “You don’t have to be a career YouTuber to do this.”His early fundraising efforts showed the potential of that idea. A 24-hour stream that started with a $1,000 target had become a much larger charitable platform within a few years. Markiplier’s 20 million subscriber milestone led to an unusual calendar projectBy March 2018, Markiplier's YouTube following was nearing 20 million subscribers. He had previously said that reaching the milestone would call for something more unusual than the gaming videos, sketches and challenges his fans knew him for.His idea was a calendar.Mark created a calendar featuring himself nude poses. The project carried the tongue-in-cheek name “Tasteful Nudes” and kept the presentation humorous and PG-13. He sold the calendar through his online shop and donated the proceeds to the Cancer Research Institute.The response was far beyond a typical merchandise project. CRI reported that the calendar campaign raised nearly $500,000 in donations in just two days. The institute's supporter page records the amount as $500,000.The fundraiser showed just how much Markiplier's audience had grown since his first charity stream. In 2012, about 2,000 subscribers helped him reach a $1,000 target. In 2018, his audience had grown to more than 20 million subscribers, and a single unusual charity project generated $500,000 for cancer research.Mark also had to sign a large number of calendars for supporters. CRI even referred to the “pain of signing all those calendars” when it spoke about the fundraiser.The project worked because it matched Markiplier's personality while keeping the focus on the charity. He used an unusual idea to capture his audience's attention and direct the resulting support toward cancer research.Markiplier’s personal connection to cancer shaped his support for CRIThe $500,000 fundraiser was not Markiplier's first time supporting the Cancer Research Institute. His 2013 livestream had already raised more than $8,000 for the organisation.His family's experience with cancer gave the cause a personal meaning. Mark had lost his father to lung cancer years before his YouTube career reached its later heights.When discussing cancer research, Mark acknowledged how difficult the disease can be while also expressing hope for future progress.“I don’t think we’re going to cure cancer anytime soon,” he said, “but the only way we’re ever going to get there is to keep working toward it.”Mark also took care when choosing charities for his fundraising efforts. According to CRI, he checked charity ratings through Charity Navigator and reviewed financial information to see how organisations used donations. At the time, he noted that CRI had received four out of four stars from Charity Navigator.His approach went beyond simply asking millions of followers to donate. Mark wanted to understand the organisations he supported and encourage his audience to become involved in causes that mattered to them.By the time CRI profiled him in January 2019, Markiplier had raised more than $3 million for charities through his online fundraising efforts.The journey from his first $1,000 charity stream in 2012 to the $500,000 calendar fundraiser in 2018 showed how quickly his charitable reach had expanded. What began with a small gaming community eventually became a fundraising platform capable of generating hundreds of thousands of dollars for cancer research.In Markiplier's case, the growth of his audience created an opportunity to do more than entertain. It gave him a way to turn the support of millions of fans into real contributions toward causes that carried a deeply personal meaning for him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: European states, Canada, Japan and UN back ICC against US sanctions
articles.summary: Several US allies call to ‘defend’ and ‘protect’ the ICC following Washington’s decision to sanction the judiciary body.
articles.body:
The United States has imposed a new set of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), prompting several countries – including US allies – to condemn the move and reiterate their support for the world’s war crimes tribunal.

On Friday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Washington would be banning transactions with the “rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate”, adding that President Donald Trump would “never allow” the Hague to prosecute Americans.

The ICC was created in 2002 to prosecute individuals accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when national authorities are unable or unwilling to do so.

The US Treasury Department announced the penalties with a six-month initial grace period and other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecommunications, software, pension payments and transactions related to detainees.

Rubio said the sanctions would give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns and would be adjusted if they did not meet those demands.

The Trump administration says the court has exceeded its authority by pursuing officials from countries that are not ICC members, such as Israel. The United States and Israel have never joined the court.

In response to the sanctions, the ICC said that the move was an “assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order”. It called on its 125 member states to defend the institution.

“The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” the ICC said in a statement. “This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment.”

The Trump administration sanctioned more than a dozen judges and prosecutors before issuing sanctions on the court itself Friday.

Allies ‘regret and disagree’ with US move

Soon after the US announcement, top United Nations officials condemned the move.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was “deeply alarmed” by the expected impact of the sanctions on the court as a whole, particularly its ability to carry out its mandate, a statement from his spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said.

“Today’s decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar,” the statement added.

UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk called for immediate measures to protect the ICC. “These sanctions – the latest in a series of retaliatory steps against the ICC and its personnel for the work they do every day to advance accountability for the very worst violations of human rights – are unacceptable,” he said.

ICC member states that are US allies also expressed dismay at the decision.

Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, whose country hosts the ICC, said the US’s decision was “deeply regrettable”.

“We will stand firm in defence of the court. At the same time, it’s important to note that the sanctions will not take effect immediately and that service providers can continue to work for the ICC. The six-month period before the sanctions take effect creates scope for dialogue,” he said.

In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Britain, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan said they “regret and strongly disagree” with the sanctions.

“If put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court’s work, its dedicated staff and their families … We remain both united in our support for the ICC and committed to engaging in constructive and inclusive dialogue with non-States Parties,” they said.

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot also said Brussels would discuss support for the ICC with European Union foreign affairs colleagues on Monday and at the upcoming European Council.

“We will press for concrete protection. The court’s independence cannot depend on whom it investigates. Europe must act. Belgium is calling for the activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the court,” Prevot said.

Similarly, organisations and rights groups sounded the alarm over the implications of the US decision.

Philippe Bolopion, executive director of US-based Human Rights Watch, said the Trump administration had made clear its aim to “destroy” the ICC and “shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court”.

“The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, is above the law. Governments that value human rights and accountability should condemn this outrageous move and take swift action to protect the ICC, its staff, and all those who cooperate with it, starting with the European Union using its laws to mitigate the sanctions’ impact in the region,” he said.

The Executive Director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, James Goldston, said the sanctions were a “calculated attack on the rule of law and the principles of judicial independence and equality that underpin it.”

“This is the latest move in a campaign of coercion intended to destroy the system of international justice,” he said.

Amnesty International called on countries to “resist”. Trump’s “sanctions are designed to isolate and ultimately destroy the International Criminal Court”, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty’s senior director for research, policy, advocacy and campaigns, said in a statement. “This existential attack must fail. States must take concrete action to resist the imposition of these measures.”

Amid widespread criticism, Israel commended the US move.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailed the sanctions and praised Trump and Rubio for taking this “critical decision”.

“The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty,” Netanyahu wrote on X.

In 2024 the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu on war crimes and crimes against humanity charges for the war on Gaza.

articles.title: Drumcree: Secretary of state Sir Chris Bryant to ban the Drumcree parade
articles.summary: The parade has led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has said he will ban the contentious Orange Order parade at Drumcree.

The dispute has led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.

Sir Chris said the chief constable advised him "it would not be possible to enable the procession to happen without a major intervention which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland".

His decision has been welcomed by Sinn Féin and the SDLP, but DUP leader Gavin Robinson said he now needs to "explain what his government intends to do to restore confidence in the rule of law".

The move comes on the 13th day of deadlock between residents and the local district lodge of the Orange Order.

The Parades Commission had ruled that the march, on Sunday 27 September, could go ahead with restrictions in place.

But the parade, from Drumcree Church into Portadown, did not happen due to a large protest on the Garvaghy Road.

Under legislation, a secretary of state can overturn a Parades Commission determination, especially following input from the police.

Sir Chris had been coming under increasing pressure from Sinn Féin and the SDLP to stop the parade.

Chief Constable Jon Boutcher had asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination allowing the parade.

On Friday night, Sir Chris said: "The Parades Commission have advised me that while ultimately a matter for the courts to determine, the commission is of the view that, in light of this current assessment by the chief constable, the original determination does not now have enduring legal effect.

"Consequently, and in the interests of wider public interest and safety, I've come to the conclusion that the circumstances under which that decision was made have now changed considerably.

"As a result, the procession cannot go ahead as it was determined."

Speaking about Sir Chris' decision, Boutcher said he had outlined to the secretary of state his "current assessment was that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession had been exhausted".

"Any remaining options would have required a substantial public order intervention," he said.

He added: "Further to this, such an operation would in my view have had not only catastrophic long-term consequences for trust and confidence in policing, but for the Northern Ireland Executive and the peace process."

In a statement, the Parades Commission said it "recognises the importance of resolving the issues arising from this dispute and hopes that a way forward can be found through constructive engagement between those concerned".

Earlier, First Minister Michelle O'Neill confirmed she had received a letter from police investigating protests over the Drumcree parading dispute.

On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.

There were jubilant scenes at a community hall off Garvaghy Road as the decision over the Drumcree parade was confirmed.

Speaking outside the centre, Breandán Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition (GRRC) said that "while this is a win for us tonight, it is one that is still tinged with sadness and with loss".

"There's no real cause for celebration that we have to remember the price that was paid to get this decision over many years."

One woman was heard saying: "Best news we've had in years," while another shouted: "No going back."

Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald said the overwhelming sense on the road was "one of relief and one of joy", adding that this "awful threat and this sense of menace has been lifted from the community".

"To have had the prospect of a march down the road was just incomprehensible, nobody could believe that this decision had been landed and the community said from the get go that they would stand strong and united and that they would not have it and they have. Right has won out here."

The Portadown District said the "chief constable has abdicated his responsibility for policing Northern Ireland".

"We further note that the secretary of state has bowed to the republican mob, and rewarded criminality. Again, the consequences should be self-evident," they said.

They said that they "understand the immense anger which is tonight engulfing our community", but appealed for calm.

In a statement on social media, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson said emergency judicial proceedings were being prepared against the secretary of state.

Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said "it has been clear in recent days that due to the actions of Sinn Féin and the total disregard for the recent determination in favour of a parade that the PSNI cannot ensure the safe completion of the parade".

"The decision of the chief constable to refer the matter to the secretary of state and his conclusion that the parade cannot proceed is a direct result of republican agitation, mobilisation and the looming threats of potential violence."

On Friday night, Orange Order members again walked to police lines at Drumcree, as they have done regularly over the past two weeks, but were halted.

Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said the announcement was a "shameful surrender... to mob rule".

However, Alliance deputy leader Eóin Tennyson said the intervention "should now create the space to get this dispute off the streets and into a political process".

Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna also welcomed the decision and said the parade "should never have been given permission in the first place and it never should again".

Ulster Unionist Party leader Jon Burrows said a "legal right" had been "defeated by an unlawful blockade".

Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin said in a post on social media that the announcement by Sir Chris would come as a significant relief to the community on the Garvaghy Road".

There has been stalemate in Portadown since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road on 27 September.

That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west.

Since then, residents have maintained a constant presence around the road while Orangemen have also repeatedly tried to march the route before being turned back by police.

The chief constable said last week that the consequences of police forcing an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road "could be catastrophic".

He had said while the PSNI's objective was to facilitate the determination, this could not be done "at all costs".

As of last Thursday, the policing operation over the dispute had cost about £3m.

Two weeks ago exactly, the Parades Commission issued a determination saying that the Orange Order parade was to be allowed on the Garvaghy Road with restrictions in place.

That prompted a legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition which opposed the march.

The Court of Appeal is considering whether to allow a challenge to the Parades Commission's ruling, which has been lodged by residents.

Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.

Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades.

Earlier this year the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place after its original decision to stop the march was overturned in court.

'Any decision is going to cause anger on one side or the other'

History shows there are no easy options when it comes to the Drumcree parade dispute.

Opinions are so deeply divided that any decision is going to cause anger on one side or the other.

Portadown Orange Order and their supporters are furious at the latest turn of events.

Exactly two weeks ago, it was the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition and their supporters who were enraged, by the original decision on the Drumcree parade.

That fury did not turn into violence on the streets.

The hope is that the outcome is the same this time.

With the Portadown parade dispute causing so much tension in recent weeks, politicians know that there is still a need to keep searching for a lasting solution.

At the moment, with feelings running so high, that looks impossible.

articles.title: Michigan Senate debate between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers spotlights anti-Muslim rhetoric as midterms race heats up
articles.summary: "You going after my mom?" El-Sayed shot back as Rogers seemed to imply his opponent might have a family member on a "watchlist".
articles.body:
A no-holds-barred televised debate between Michigan Senate rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers has highlighted how ugly personal attacks are ramping up in the US midterms elections race.

In Thursday evening's duel, Rogers questioned whether someone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist". El-Sayed, a Democrat, called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration".

Moderator Rick Albin said the barbs continued off camera, spilling into the commercial break - something Albin said he has never seen in 30 years of doing debates.

On the morning after the debate, US President Donald Trump posted on social media attacking the Democrat and bringing up his Muslim identity.

The Michigan race could affect which party controls the Senate after November's midterm elections as Democrats campaign to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from the Republicans.

Little was considered off limits in the verbal jousting between Rogers and El-Sayed, which saw the Republican repeatedly suggest the Democrat and his family had ties to terrorist organisations.

El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, denied this.

A fact-check from a state news outlet, Bridge Michigan, has said there is no evidence that El-Sayed is personally connected to the Muslim Brotherhood, branches of which have been designated as terrorist organisations by the US.

The Democrat questioned whether Rogers was even from Michigan and labelled his opponent a "Florida man", with yachts and a mansion in the Sunshine State. Rogers denied the Florida ties and boat ownership.

"Weak, cowardly, won't stand up until his poll numbers drop," El-Sayed said during one heated exchange.

The economy, immigration and support for Israel were topics that came up as expected during the debate.

But tensions flared as Rogers appeared to attack El-Sayed's family.

The rivals were discussing Flock cameras, the controversial AI-powered surveillance system, which El-Sayed said should be federally regulated.

"And why would that bother you?" Rogers shot back. "Well, if you have someone in your family that might be on the watchlist."

El-Sayed challenged Rogers to "go ahead and say it", adding: "Are you going after my mom?"

The Democrat's mother, Fatten Elkomy, previously worked as a nurse practitioner for the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA), according to the Midwesterner , a conservative regional news outlet.

The US treasury department designated IARA in 2004 for supporting terrorism.

The US justice department charged figures within IARA in 2007 with illegal wire transfers to Iraq, but El-Sayed's mother was not among those indicted and she left the agency in 2004.

The BBC has contacted El-Sayed's campaign and Elkomy for comment.

One academic told the BBC that Thursday's debate underscores how anti-Muslim sentiment is becoming increasingly normalised at the highest level of US politics.

Quardricos Driskell, a George Washington University political science professor, pointed to the period after the 9/11 attacks as a time when there was similar rhetoric, but he noted the distinction in presidential leadership.

In the wake of the attacks, then-President George W Bush stood in front of a mosque and defended the Muslim faith, saying: "Islam is peace."

Driskell said: "Islamophobia has long existed, I think across American political society from both parties.

"What distinguishes the current moment is that the explicit use of Muslim identity as a political attack is by prominent Republican leaders."

On Friday morning, President Trump issued the latest in a series of attacks on the Democrat.

"Mohammad is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country," Trump wrote on social media.

Some questioned why Trump chose to refer to El-Sayed as Mohammad - his full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El‑Sayed, but he has been known as Abdul since kindergarten, according to the Detroit News .

Trump's comment follows several other similar anti-Muslim remarks from elected officials, including Tennessee Republican congressman Andy Ogles posting on X earlier this year: "Muslim's don't belong in American society."

After Zohran Mamdani was elected as the first ever Muslim mayor of New York City, he faced similar attacks.

"After 9/11 we said 'Never Forget.' I think we sadly have forgotten," Republican congresswoman Nancy Mace wrote on X, after Mamdani's election.

Gregg Nunziata, a Republican policy adviser, told the BBC these types of comments were "extremely destructive and deeply alarming".

He also noted the absence of condemnation for these remarks, saying it's "the responsibility of leaders to tamp down that type of rhetoric and police their own side and that's not happening today".

There has been a rise in anti-Muslim sentiment across the US, according to the Pew Research Center.

In 2002, 25% of adults said Islam "is more likely" to encourage violence than other religions. That number jumped to 51% in 2026.

It comes amid a rise in hatred more broadly in the US, including antisemitism.

Haris Tarin, vice-president of the Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC), said Trump's comments like his social media post on Friday morning make him feel "sick".

He said his organisation had tracked an eight-fold increase in anti-Muslim speech over the last year.

"This rise has coincided with elections, and it has allowed for candidates who oppose American Muslims licence to openly attack their faith," Tarin said.

Driskell said such attacks often exploit voters' fears.

"We have to keep in mind the motivating factor often in politics, and particularly during campaigning, which is fear," he said.

"That's what ultimately Islamophobia is - the fear," he continued, "instilling fear that people get out and vote".

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot plotted ‘suicide’ attack on Israel, UAE says
articles.summary: Attorney General says suspect admitted he acted alone after preparing ‌‌psychologically ‌‌and physically for the attack.
articles.body:
Authorities in the United Arab Emirates say the co-pilot who tried to seize control of a Flydubai aircraft on September 30 was on a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv.

Emirati public prosecutors believe the plan “drew inspiration from the 9/11 attack”, Attorney General Hamad ⁠⁠Saif al-Shamsi said in a statement carried by state news agency WAM on Friday, referring to the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.

WAM reported al-Shamsi’s comments as well as updates on what Emirati investigators had discovered about the alleged plot after launching an inquiry into the incident on October 1.

They found that the ⁠⁠29-year-old suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route and the ⁠⁠airport”, WAM reported.

The attorney general said the suspect had worked for several airlines in ‌‌different countries, including Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, before ‌‌joining ‌‌Flydubai in January.

Investigators examined Flydubai’s recruiting procedures and found the suspect had met all professional and security requirements, including holding a pilot’s licence and providing a certificate of good conduct.

“However, none of the procedures revealed any ⁠⁠indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot,” the statement said.

Al-Shamsi’s statement did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing, and contained the most detailed account yet from prosecutors about what they believe to have happened.

UAE officials ‌‌have not identified the suspect, who is accused of attacking his co-pilot, the captain of the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight that was carrying 174 people on board. But people with direct knowledge of the matter have identified him as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, both the Reuters and Associated Press news agencies reported.

Al-Shamsi said the suspect had told investigators he had prepared ‌‌psychologically ‌‌and physically for the attack by viewing material promoting “terrorism” and taking boxing lessons.

The findings indicated that “signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia”, the statement said.

It added that the suspect “admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others”, and that he “provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution” in the presence of his lawyer.

At 7:05am (03:05 GMT) on September 30, Flight FZ1073 departed Dubai for Tel Aviv, climbing to 34,000ft (more than 10,300 metres), according to Flightradar24. A little more than two hours later, it suddenly began a steep descent.

Flight-tracking data showed the plane plunging more than 17,000 feet in about two minutes, before climbing and descending again.

A fight had begun in the cockpit between the two pilots after the co-pilot stabbed the Indian captain of the plane, Smit Machchhar.

Machchhar later described finding himself seriously wounded on the cockpit floor as the aircraft descended.

Passengers and crew members reportedly entered the cabin and overpowered the co-pilot. The aircraft eventually levelled out at about 15,000 feet. Its transponder was subsequently switched to code 7500, signalling unlawful interference.

Two reserve pilots who were on board took control of the jet and landed it in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia. The plane landed safely at 9:45am local time (06:45 GMT).

Saudi authorities said both pilots were taken to hospital and were later transferred to Abu Dhabi after being medically cleared.

articles.title: Green Cards reflect cases started years ago: Immigration attorney raises 5 points on Trump administration's PERM ban
articles.summary: Suspending the Green Card process of eight tech companies and accusing them of depriving American workers are two different things that have been put
articles.body: Suspending the Green Card process of eight tech companies and accusing them of depriving American workers are two different things that have been put together, experts felt after Vice President JD Vance's announcement. Vance cited 6,000 American layoffs and compared it with 6,300 H-1B approvals and 3,000 Green Cards. But do they show that foreign workers replaced the Americans who lost their jobs? Immigration attorney Gnanamookan Senthurjothi asked as he raised 5 points on the correlation.H-1B is a non-immigrant work visa and PERM is a step in the Green Card process that gives permanent residency to the applicants. H-1Bs often take the employment-based Green Card route to become permanent residents of the US. But they are not directly linked without context.H-1B approvals do not equal new hiresSenthurjothi said H-1B approvals do not always mean new hires -- there are extensions or change of status for existing employees. "Microsoft has said that about 80% of its H-1B filings last fiscal year were extensions or changes of status for existing employees. An extension is not a new hire, and an amendment is not necessarily a new job. These categories cannot be added together and treated as replacements," he said.One lay-off, one hiring: Different skills, different responsibilitiesThe attorney argued that many specialized roles exist in tech companies and the role of one laid-off employee in one team does not always match with a foreign professional who was not laid off. They may have different skills and responsibilities and role-level evidence is needed before concluding that one replaced another.Green Card cases are oldSenthurjothi explained that the Green Card queue is so long for Indian that the individuals who are getting Green Cards now filed for applications around 2013-2014. So 3,000 Green Cards now does not mean they have been hired now. Most employment-based Green Cards go to people already working for the sponsoring employer, often for years. PERM labor certification, where required, is filed long before the final approval," he said.Redressal for displacementThe attorney said that there is already a provision to address displacement by an employer. "In PERM, an employer that laid off U.S. workers in the same or a related occupation within six months before filing must notify and consider those workers," he said.Correlation is not proof of replacement"Layoffs and approvals can fall in the same reporting period without involving the same jobs, teams or individuals. The Department of Labor is entitled to investigate suspected violations, and if employers made false certifications or unlawfully disadvantaged American workers, the evidence should determine the consequences. The numbers may justify asking questions. They do not, by themselves, answer them," he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Dad banned from school grounds after protesting trans runner competing against his daughter
articles.summary: Sierra Retzlaff and Charlie Garrett walked off a Washington state cross country race to protest a biological male competing in girls sports.
articles.body: On Sept. 5, a cross country athlete and a student at Camas High in Washington State finished 76th in a JV cross country race. On Sept. 29, he finished first in a varsity race in a meet against Union High school. Did he recover from an injury? Train himself back into shape? No. Midway through the season, he decided he was going to start running as a girl. Under the rules of the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association (WIAA), which governs high school sports in the state, such a switch is permitted. This is what allowed the trans athlete to also finish second among 195 girls in a Sept. 26 race in Portland. WASHINGTON OFFICIALS WON'T BUDGE ON TRANS ATHLETE POLICY AFTER GIRL FILES SCOTUS APPEAL FOR ALLEGED ASSAULT But as you might imagine, not everybody competing against the trans athlete is on board with all this. Last month, two girls and a father decided to protest — which ultimately led to the dad being served a criminal trespass notice. Sierra Retzlaff and Charlie Garrett are cross country runners for Skyview High in Vancouver, WA. A week before their meet against Camas, the two girls found out that they would be racing against a boy. After some discussion, they decided that they were going to make a statement. How? By walking up to the starting line with body paint reading "keep women in women's sports" ... and walking off once the race began. This prompted mixed reactions. Retzlaff said that she has received a lot of support but has also had friends that started ignoring her. One man that absolutely had her back, however, was her father — Joel Retzlaff. Retzlaff and his wife brought two signs to the Sept. 15 meet. The first read: "It will never be OK for a XY to steal an opportunity from a XX." The second read: "Please only XX competing with XX, XY competing with XY. Keep it fair." FEMALE ATHLETES, WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATES SPEAK ON CAPITOL HILL AS TRANS ATHLETE ISSUE HOVERS OVER MIDTERMS But WIAA has a no-signage rule (aside from team banners), so Camas' athletic director Stephen Baranowski approached Retzlaff and asked him to leave. Retzlaff asked why, and Baranowski explained to him it was because of the signage. Retzlaff agreed to take the signs down, but he still wanted to make his voice heard. So as he walked back to his car after Sierra's race, he held up his sign and chanted "Keep boys out of girls sports!" And after he got into his car, he drove by the venue, honked his horn and repeated the same chant while his friend held the signs out the window. The consequence? A criminal trespass notice that keeps Retzlaff off Camas school district properties for the next year. That may seem like an emotional reaction from the Camas school district, but its superintendent, John Anzalone, insists it wasn't. It was relayed to him that Retzlaff drove through a "barrier" — essentially an area closed off by construction tape — and that the trespass notice was in the interest of safety. Retzlaff said that Anzalone's perspective is "valid," but it doesn't sound like he has any regrets. In his mind, he was standing up for girls in a way that most parents didn't. Retzlaff's response to critics? "I would beg to ask them where all the adults are that know the difference between a boy and a girl and why they're letting this happen." Garrett, one of the students who walked off, said the trans athlete's mother followed her around and recorded her for much of the meet. Apparently, she didn't stand down when Garrett's mother, Emily Sadowski, confronted her and told her to stop filming. ACTIVISTS UNLEASH A 'NEXT WAVE' BALLOT STRATEGY FOR WOMEN'S SPORTS INSIDE DEEP BLUE STATES But like Joel, Charlie isn't second-guessing her decision to stand up for girls "I thought it was more important to show how this is affecting me and all the girls in our district," said Garrett, adding that she doesn't have any hate toward the trans athlete. "It comes down to biology and the spots being taken away from Sierra, me and all the girls." On Nov. 3, Washington voters will decide whether to ban biological boys from competing in K-12 girls’ sports through Initiative 638. It would be the first time the public passed a law enforcing such separation. articles.title: Second defendant in Cornell fraternity case seeks New York AG’s recusal
articles.summary: Attorneys representing Winston Lee, one of the former fraternity members accused in the Cornell University sexual assault lawsuit, filed a motion Friday in criminal court seeking to disqualify New York Attorney General Letitia James from any future grand jury proceedings.
articles.body: Attorneys representing Winston Lee, one of the former fraternity members accused in the Cornell University sexual assault lawsuit, filed a motion Friday in criminal court seeking to disqualify New York Attorney General Letitia James from any future grand jury proceedings. The motion — filed by attorneys Teny Geragos, Marc Agnifilo and Jacob Kaplan — asked a judge to preclude James from conducting a criminal investigation into whether former Chi Phi members, including Lee, engaged in sexual assault in October 2024. Lee’s attorneys argued that the Tompkins County court has the authority to step in if necessary to ensure the fairness of a grand jury process. They are asking for any future potential grand jury panelists to be polled on whether they are aware of James’ comments. They also asked for the court to schedule arguments on the issue. In response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for James’ office said: “In this and every investigation, the Office of the Attorney General is committed to conducting a comprehensive review of nothing but the facts, the evidence, and the law.” The filing follows a separate legal effort by lawyers for Cornell defendant Gillio Lopes, who earlier this week filed a civil court motion asking a judge for the same relief: the dismissal of James following her appointment as special counsel by Gov. Kathy Hochul. Jane Doe’s civil suit was filed last month against seven fraternity members as well as Cornell, the Chi Phi fraternity and her sorority. The lawsuit alleges that both Lee and Lopes did drugs off her body and sexually assaulted her. Lee’s and Lopes’ attorneys say their clients deny the accusations brought against them. Two of the other men named in the suit have also denied separate allegations against them. None of the men named has been criminally charged. Cornell has said that it welcomes new investigations into the case. The fraternity and sorority previously declined to discuss the pending litigation. It also marks the first time the well-known legal team, which has handled a number of significant sexual misconduct matters, publicly acknowledged representing one of the men accused by a former Cornell student who filed a lawsuit last month under the pseudonym Jane Doe. Hochul and James “have together created a blatant appearance of impropriety that, combined with the AG’s ethical violations, should lead to the AG’s recusal,” Geragos wrote in a motion filed in criminal court in Tompkins County, the upstate New York area where Cornell is located. Geragos pointed to social media comments posted by James as Jane Doe’s lawsuit captured national attention. “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable,” James wrote prior to her appointment as special prosecutor. “To her and all other survivors: You’re not alone. We stand with you.” Lawyers for Lee and Lopes argue the remarks show that James prejudged the case and is unfit to conduct an impartial review of the matter. An Oct. 29 hearing has been set in Lopes’ case for James’ office to argue that her appointment should not be voided. “The public needs confidence that the person directing this investigation will evaluate the evidence with an open mind,” Lopes’ attorney, Andrew Miltenberg, said in a statement on Friday. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten vowed to present evidence to a grand jury prior to James’ office taking on the probe. Van Houten previously found that Jane Doe had not described a prosecutable crime in a six-page statement provided to police in November 2024 and ruled out the possibility of charges. Jane Doe told police that she engaged in a consensual threesome on the evening in question, but that events spiraled as she became increasingly incapacitated and more men became involved. Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for Jane Doe, has previously said that sex assault victims sometimes do not immediately recognize the coercive nature of an encounter because they rationalize aspects of a traumatic event. Geragos’ law firm, Agnifilo Intrater LLP, previously represented hip-hop mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs and Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein in high-profile criminal trials. Combs, 56, was acquitted in July 2025 on one count of racketeering conspiracy and two counts of sex trafficking by force, fraud or coercion. The jury found him guilty on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. The rapper and record producer was sentenced to 50 months in federal prison. The jury in Weinstein’s third trial failed to reach a unanimous verdict on a third-degree rape charge involving Jessica Mann, a former aspiring actor. The judge declared a mistrial in May. In a separate trial last year, the former Miramax chief was convicted on a count of first-degree criminal sexual act involving Miriam “Mimi” Haley, a former “Project Runway” production assistant. He was recently sentenced to 15 years in prison. Marc Agnifilo and his wife, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, represent Luigi Mangione, the 28-year-old accused of fatally shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. Mangione in August pleaded not guilty to federal stalking charges, kicking off a double jeopardy fight in New York state court, where he still faces murder charges.

articles.title: UN envoy warns Yemen has returned to ‘full-scale war’, urges dialogue
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised gov’t urge UN Security Council action amid Houthi escalation.
articles.body:
United Nations Special Envoy to Yemen Hans Grundberg says that the country has slid back into “full-scale war” as fighting between the Houthis and internationally recognised government forces continues.

During a meeting at the UN Security Council on Friday to discuss the situation in Yemen, Grundberg said civilians, including women and children, were bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”.

“Ongoing instability in the Middle East continues to impact dynamics in Yemen, while developments in Yemen, in turn, reverberate across the region,” he said.

“Regional security, freedom of navigation and the protection of international trade are legitimate concerns that must be addressed. International engagement on Yemen must also be grounded in the realities of Yemen and the needs and aspirations of its people,” Grundberg added.

The envoy stressed that “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now.”

“Ultimately, gains on the battlefield cannot substitute for the negotiations that will be required to settle the conflict,” he said, urging Security Council members to collectively support mediation efforts.

According to the UN, at least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others have been injured since August, with children bearing a disproportionate toll during the ongoing clashes.

The UN representative for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Abdullah Ali Fadhel al-Saadi, told the Security Council that the threat from the Houthis was no longer an “internal Yemeni affair”.

Al-Saadi called on the council to take “decisive, practical measures” to reduce the flow of funding, weapons and technology to the Iranian-backed group and also strengthen cooperation with the Yemeni government.

He thanked Riyadh, which supports the government, for “standing beside the Yemeni people and their government, and for their continued support to state institutions and our economy”.

This comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continue, with the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority reporting on Friday that the King Khalid International Airport, north of Riyadh, was subjected to two attacks on Thursday, in which three Saudi citizens were killed.

Gulf states and European countries have condemned the attack on the airport, with Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs calling it “unacceptable”.

During the council meeting, Saudi Arabia’s UN representative, Abdulaziz al-Wasil, said the UN body must address the “dangerous escalation” ongoing in Yemen.

“These rapid developments in Yemen and the continued escalation by the terrorist Houthi militias must be addressed by the Council,” al-Wasil said.

Al-Wasil added that Riyadh will “not allow Yemen to be turned into a staging ground for threats to its security or to the freedom of navigation”.

articles.title: Three men found guilty of murdering two Australian surfer brothers and US friend
articles.summary: The bodies of Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad were found  at the bottom of a well.
articles.body:
Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.

Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús are yet to be sentenced - but they are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a Mexican prison.

Debra Robinson, the brother's mother, told the courtroom in the northern Baja California state the murders of her sons had taken "the future we had imagined with them".

During the trial the court heard the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area. Their bodies were later found with gunshot wounds to their heads, dumped down a well.

The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence in other parts of Mexico.

Debra Robinson and her husband Martin Robinson have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial and they delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict.

"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," said Martin.

Family members of Rhoad joined the trial by video link.

Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".

During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús "El Kekas" Gerardo, was sentenced in a separate trial to twenty years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.

At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.

The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers and the chilling murders revealed much about how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.

The only explanation the authorities appeared able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Their killings took place barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them.

At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to commemorate the men by paddling out at one of the area's best known surfing spots and throwing flowers into the sea.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

Amid the demands for action, Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence in her state.

"Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said.

"I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

articles.title: Attorney for alleged victim of trans athlete sexual assault says SCOTUS fight can help set Title IX precedent
articles.summary: Kallie Keeler's Supreme Court wrestling case could force 23 states to restrict transgender athletes in girls' sports under Title IX, her lawyer says.
articles.body: A Washington high school wrestler’s Supreme Court fight could help bring restrictions on transgender athletes in girls’ sports to 23 states, an attorney representing her told OutKick. Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF) senior counsel Hal Frampton said the ultimate objective is a ruling establishing that Title IX requires a protected female sports category, with consequences beyond the immediate request to protect wrestler Kallie Keeler. "And the hope would be then that that would force all 23 of those states to enact policies protecting women and girls, protecting the female category, and simply getting back to the common sense notion that women's sports are for women," Frampton said. WASHINGTON FAMILY REQUESTS SCOTUS INJUNCTION AFTER DAUGHTER WAS ALLEGEDLY SEXUALLY ASSAULTED BY TRANS ATHLETE Keeler, identified in court as K.M.K., and her mother, Stephanie Lynne Brown, are seeking intervention after Keeler alleged she was sexually assaulted by a transgender opponent during a girls’ wrestling match in December 2025. "Ultimately, the goal is a ruling from the Supreme Court that says that Title IX requires fairness and safety for women and girls," Frampton said. Asked whether that broader objective could be accomplished through the current Supreme Court application or would require further steps, Frampton called it "a huge step toward accomplishing that goal." The application seeks an injunction pending appeal and alternatively asks the justices to take up the case before the Ninth Circuit finishes reviewing it. A temporary order protecting Keeler would not, by itself, impose new eligibility policies on 23 states. INSIDE THE SUPREME COURT BATTLE TO 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' The distinction matters because the Ninth Circuit said the Supreme Court’s recent West Virginia v. B.P.J. decision left open whether schools may allow biological males who identify as female to participate in girls’ and women’s sports. Frampton’s goal would address that unresolved question. For Keeler, Frampton said, the immediate concern is returning to wrestling before her remaining high school seasons slip away. "We filed the emergency application with the Supreme Court because it's really the only way to get Callie and her family relief in advance of wrestling season," he said. Frampton emphasized that the emergency request seeks protection for Keeler rather than monetary damages, though he left open the possibility of pursuing damages later. "For right now, all we're saying is while this case is pending," give her assurance she can compete without being matched against a male athlete, he said. He accused Washington officials of refusing to compromise: "From the very beginning, there's been no effort to compromise, to accommodate Callie, to appreciate what she's been through." Justice Elena Kagan has requested a response to the application by 4 p.m. EDT Oct. 13. The request remained pending as of Friday. Washington’s wrestling season begins in mid-November. The Ninth Circuit denied emergency relief Sept. 25, finding the family had not established an immediate emergency or a sufficiently strong likelihood of success. It also raised concerns about other students’ privacy and the breadth of the requested relief, while noting the district had said Keeler could forfeit matches without district-imposed adverse consequences. Frampton rejected the privacy justification and accused Washington officials of refusing to accommodate Keeler. "From the very beginning, there's been no effort to compromise, to accommodate Callie, to appreciate what she's been through," he said. The WIAA previously said it would follow state law allowing participation by gender identity and revise its policies if that law changes. Pierce County prosecutors declined to charge Keeler’s opponent, concluding they could not prove third-degree rape beyond a reasonable doubt or overcome a consent defense arising from case law on athletic contests. The prosecutor emphasized that the decision did not mean approval of the alleged conduct. Frampton said the experience has taken a toll on Keeler and her family, including her transfer to another school. "She ultimately had to change schools in order to get away from the harassment and bullying and the just lack of concern from the administration, which is not easy for any high school student to do," he said. Still, he described the family as determined to continue pursuing the case. "High school careers are fleeting. She's already a junior. Blink and it'll be over. And we just don't want her to miss out on the opportunity to compete in high school athletics," Frampton said. The family’s request has drawn support from 24 states, led by Iowa and Idaho, which filed a brief Oct. 7 arguing that allowing biological males into female sports denies girls Title IX protections. The Independent Council on Women’s Sports (ICONS) and its members also filed an amicus brief Oct. 8 supporting Keeler’s emergency request, arguing that school administrators bear responsibility under Title IX for protecting female athletes. The brief contends that lost athletic opportunities cause irreparable harm and that privacy concerns should not prevent schools from identifying competitors’ biological sex. OutKick reached out to the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association, Puyallup School District and the Washington Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction for comment on Frampton’s latest statements. In its previous response to the injunction request, the WIAA said it would continue following Washington law allowing students to compete according to their gender identity and could revise its policies if the law changes. The superintendent’s office said it does not oversee athletics but is responsible for communicating and enforcing applicable law. articles.title: Latest Guernsey cruise passenger figures 'encouraging' for sector
articles.summary: Guernsey Ports says 28,000 cruise passengers are expected to visit the island this year.
articles.body:
Guernsey Ports officials say the number of cruise passengers visiting the island this year has provided "encouraging signs" that the sector is expanding again.

Mark Renouf, cruise operations and business development manager, said 2026 was the first year passenger numbers had stabilised year-on-year since the pandemic and were expected to reach 28,000.

He said there were already 63 cruise bookings for 2027, compared with 51 in 2026, as well as an increase in overall ship capacity of about 8,000 passengers.

"While we are still some way from the levels seen before Covid, this season has provided encouraging signs that our cruise sector is moving in the right direction," Renouf said.

Renouf said a scheme bringing local stallholders into the cruise area on busy ship days had "helped create a more memorable welcome experience for visitors while providing another opportunity for local producers to benefit from cruise tourism".

"Cruise lines plan their itineraries years in advance, so building relationships and raising Guernsey's profile within the industry is essential," he said.

"The work that has taken place over the past few years is beginning to deliver results, with new cruise lines choosing to visit Guernsey and established operators showing renewed confidence in the island."

articles.title: 'Alcohol and drugs ruined my band - I'm glad to have another chance'
articles.summary: The Temperance Movement are back with their first album in eight years, after an acrimonious break-up.
articles.body:
Phil Campbell still shudders when he recalls how his band the Temperance Movement came to a messy end.

After years of hard graft and endless gigs at home and abroad, the blues-rock group were finally tasting regular success - but Campbell had become increasingly hooked on drink and drugs.

It eventually led the Glaswegian singer to leave the band, and attempt to get his own life back on track.

Now the group have not only reunited but brought out a new album, marking a fresh chapter that at one stage seemed an unlikely prospect.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

Campbell told BBC Scotland News how the aftermath of a shambolic gig in Wales in December 2019 made him realise that the band was all but over, and that his actions may have accelerated the end.

"The last gig we did in 2019 was just so terrible that it had to be the end," he reflects.

"I had taken the band and crashed it into a wall. The way I dealt with it all made it worse and then I realised I had lost everything.

"The point at which I knew I had taken it too far was when it was too late. It was the end of the last gig and my memory of that was how quickly everyone vanished at the end of the show.

"Usually you'd finish a gig and people stayed behind to talk or celebrate, and this time they just fled."

It was a grim end to an unlikely success story.

Campbell was a Glasgow singer-songwriter type who, he jokes, took music far too seriously. The rest of the band were session musicians who had backed big names like Robbie Williams but were keen for a crack at their own songs.

When they began playing together the result was old time, full throated blues rock n' roll. Within two years an album was released, and in the 12 months after that they found themselves opening for the Rolling Stones at several shows.

"We got together in this wonderful romantic way, and it was amazing," says Campbell.

"Those early days we worked in Luke's [Potashnick, guitarist] kitchen, eating well, drinking coffee and just recording songs. We must have done hundreds of shows."

The five-piece took their name from the social movement that shuns alcohol and while band members did not go that far, they kept focused on the music as by far the most important thing.

However, Campbell had past issues with drinking too much, and as the band's fame grew and they began embarking on lengthy tours of America, his resolve wavered.

"I've always had problems with booze and drugs, since I was a young man", he says.

"A lot of people I grew up with drank too much, and played music, and you heard about all the casualties, these Scottish bands that didn't make it because the singer was a mess.

"The band was called the Temperance Movement partly because I was sober when it started and it was a reminder to stay sober, but then I found I loved getting stoned.

"When you're playing music all the time a wee bit of this or that made it more interesting and the problem is the rest of the band aren't hedonists at all, they're very measured. When I started using again it changed the whole dynamic of the band."

That led to problems that culminated on that stage in Porthcawl in 2019. The following month Campbell's departure from the group was announced.

However, after years working on other projects, the band began to stir.

A reunion tour playing old material took place in 2025, and the band felt secure enough to start plotting a new album.

The result is New Promise Land Incorporated, produced by Ethan Johns, who previously worked with the likes of Kings of Leon.

"For the comeback tour we just needed to play the old music and say hello again," says Campbell.

"But there was a bit of a wait before we could start writing again after that, just due to how everyone's lives are now."

Campbell himself is a dad of two and he jokes that fronting a rock band is his second job, behind being a taxi service for his kids.

A more serious problem emerged following the comeback tour though, after a cyst was found on his vocal chords.

"I needed to get that sorted, so I couldn't sing for two months.

"I was terrified of life as an average singer and that I wouldn't have the big voice of before, but the minute I came around I knew it was better instantly."

Back to full strength vocally, Campbell was able to join his bandmates in crafting their fourth record.

It is unlikely to surprise too many, delivering emphatic rock that is heavy on grooves and riffs.

Campbell himself makes no bones about the fact he is relishing being back on stage again, with a November tour pencilled in that includes a date at Glasgow's famed Barrowland.

Being front and centre of attention is something he loves.

"I've always been a show off, doing voices or acting or trying to show what I can do," he laughs.

"I was quite keen to get onstage and start singing and showing off again, as lead singers like to do.

"We opened on the reunion tour with us singing in harmony and playing acoustically, which is what we used to do in small venues - but to be honest, I just couldn't wait until the big drums kicked in and we got the dry ice going again."

articles.title: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
articles.summary: The US president hopes to ease his party's pain before next month's midterm elections, writes the BBC's North America correspondent.
articles.body:
Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.

Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.

The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.

As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.

Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin'

What are the US midterms? A simple guide

For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves . He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.

He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.

His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.

It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.

It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.

The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.

Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.

With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.
